Introduction

Starting a Hospice in Wisconsin represents a meaningful opportunity to serve terminally ill patients and their families while building a compliant, sustainable care business. These programs deliver compassionate, interdisciplinary care focused on comfort and quality of life. Oversight and funding are administered by the Wisconsin Department of Health Services (DHS) Division of Quality Assurance (DQA), with reimbursement and program funding coordinated through Wisconsin Medicaid, Medicare, and various Managed Care Organizations (MCOs).

With a significant state budget allocation of over $7 million for hospice and palliative care through 2025, Wisconsin demonstrates strong government support and recognition of this essential service. Reimbursement rates, such as Medicaid Routine Home Care at $33-$35 per day and a 2.8% Medicare rate increase for FY2024, create a viable financial model. This environment makes Wisconsin a stable market with established demand and significant growth opportunities, particularly for providers prepared to navigate licensing, staffing, and compliance requirements in underserved rural regions and specialized service areas.

This guide walks you through every step of launching a Hospice in Wisconsin, from understanding state and federal regulations to developing your business plan, hiring staff, and preparing for your initial licensure and certification surveys.

  • Understand Wisconsin’s Hospice Regulations

Section 1: Understand Wisconsin’s Hospice Regulations

Navigating the regulatory landscape is the first and most critical step in launching your hospice agency. Wisconsin regulates Hospice programs through the Wisconsin Department of Health Services (DHS) Division of Quality Assurance (DQA). The primary state-level rules are found in the Wisconsin Administrative Code under DHS 131, which is responsible for the full scope of hospice licensure, including standards for patient care, staffing qualifications, operational procedures, and physical environment requirements.

Because most hospice care is funded by federal programs, providers must also achieve and maintain certification from the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS). This means complying with the Medicare Conditions of Participation (CoPs) for hospice, which are the national standards for care quality and safety. Other federal frameworks like the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) are also paramount for protecting patient privacy. The state and federal regulatory framework emphasizes an interdisciplinary approach to care, patient rights, quality of life, comprehensive care planning, and robust bereavement support for families. Licenses in Wisconsin require regular renewal, typically on an annual or biennial basis, and maintaining compliance is an ongoing effort.

Section 2: Choose the Type and Size of Your Program

While all licensed hospices must be able to provide four core levels of care, your business model will likely focus on one or two as your primary service. Wisconsin supports multiple Hospice service levels, each with different staffing, logistical, and reimbursement considerations:

  • Routine Home Care (RHC): This is the most common level of hospice care, provided wherever the patient calls home—be it a private residence, an assisted living facility, or a nursing home. It includes nursing, aide, social work, and spiritual care services on an intermittent basis.
  • General Inpatient Care (GIP): This level is for managing acute pain or complex symptoms that cannot be addressed in the home setting. GIP is provided in a Medicare-certified hospital, skilled nursing facility, or dedicated inpatient hospice unit.
  • Continuous Home Care (CHC): Provided during periods of crisis to keep a patient at home, CHC involves more intensive, round-the-clock nursing care for a short duration to manage symptoms and avoid hospitalization.
  • Inpatient Respite Care: This is short-term inpatient care provided to a patient to give their primary caregivers a temporary break. It is limited to five consecutive days at a time.

Program size is measured by Average Daily Census (ADC). A new agency might start with a capacity for 20-30 patients and grow from there. While Wisconsin has over 100 licensed agencies, demand remains strong. Urban centers like Milwaukee and Madison are more competitive, but high-demand regions include the rural northern and western parts of the state. These lower-penetration regions offer significant entry opportunities. Furthermore, there is a growing need for specialized services, such as pediatric hospice, culturally tailored programs for diverse communities, and integrated palliative care services.

Section 3: Business Structure and Licensing

Before you can apply for a license, you must establish a formal business entity. Most hospice providers in Wisconsin operate as a Limited Liability Company (LLC) or an S-Corporation to create a liability shield between the business and personal assets and to take advantage of pass-through taxation.

To formalize your business and prepare for licensure, you must:

  • Register your business entity with the Wisconsin Department of Financial Institutions.
  • Obtain an Employer Identification Number (EIN) from the IRS, which is necessary for hiring employees and tax filing.
  • Secure required insurance coverage, including general liability, professional liability (malpractice), and workers’ compensation insurance.
  • Submit a comprehensive licensing application to the DHS Division of Quality Assurance (DQA). This application requires detailed information about your business structure, key personnel, proposed services, and policies and procedures.

Licensing timelines, including the crucial Medicare certification process, generally range from 6 to 12 months. The exact duration depends heavily on your readiness, the completeness of your application, and your ability to pass the required licensure and certification surveys on the first attempt.

Section 4: Develop a Comprehensive Business Plan

A robust business plan is your roadmap to a sustainable hospice agency. It should include detailed financial projections based on Wisconsin-specific data. Startup costs in Wisconsin for a hospice agency typically range from $75,000 to $300,000. This capital covers business formation, licensing fees, initial marketing, office setup, electronic medical record (EMR) software, and securing enough operating cash to cover expenses before reimbursement begins.

Operating expenses are driven primarily by payroll. Staffing represents approximately 60-70% of total costs in a hospice setting. Other major expenses include medical supplies, pharmacy costs, mileage reimbursement, insurance, and administrative overhead.

Your revenue will come from per diem payments from various payers. A typical reimbursement snapshot in Wisconsin includes:

  • Wisconsin Medicaid Routine Home Care: $33 – $35 per day
  • Wisconsin Medicaid General Inpatient Care: $130 – $140 per day
  • Medicare: Rates are set annually by CMS and vary by geographic location and level of care. For FY2024, rates saw a 2.8% increase, making them the most significant revenue source for most hospices.
  • Managed Care & Private Insurance: Rates are negotiated directly with MCOs like Inclusa, My Choice Wisconsin, and iCare, as well as private insurance companies.

With strong operational management and a focus on maintaining an average daily census at 80-90% of your target capacity, providers can generally achieve profit margins in the 5% to 15% range after an initial break-even period of 12-18 months.

Section 5: Secure a Suitable Facility or Office

Even if you plan to provide all care in patients’ homes, you must have a physical administrative office. This office serves as your operational hub and must meet specific requirements.

Facility and office requirements include:

  • An administrative office that is accessible to staff and the public and complies with local zoning ordinances.
  • Secure, locked storage for patient records and medical supplies to ensure HIPAA compliance and prevent unauthorized access.
  • A confidential space for conducting patient-related communications and team meetings.
  • If you plan to operate a dedicated inpatient unit, the facility must meet extensive state and federal health and safety codes, including fire safety, accessibility standards (ADA), patient room specifications, and nursing station requirements as outlined in DHS 131 and the Medicare CoPs.

Your location selection should be strategic. Consider proximity to key referral sources like hospitals and large physician groups, accessibility for your staff traveling throughout your service area, and the availability of a qualified clinical workforce.

Section 6: Hire and Train Qualified Staff

Hospice care is delivered by an Interdisciplinary Group (IDG), and having a complete, qualified team is a non-negotiable requirement for licensure. Your team must be in place before you can accept your first patient.

Required roles for your IDG typically include:

  • Administrator: Responsible for the day-to-day operations of the agency. In Wisconsin, this individual must hold at least a bachelor’s degree.
  • Medical Director: A licensed physician who provides medical oversight, certifies terminal illness, and consults with the IDG.
  • Registered Nurses (RNs): Act as case managers, perform skilled nursing visits, manage symptoms, and coordinate the plan of care.
  • Social Workers (MSW): Provide psychosocial support, assist with long-term planning, and connect patients and families with community resources.
  • Spiritual Counselors/Chaplains: Address the spiritual and existential needs of patients and families.
  • Bereavement Counselors: Manage the bereavement program, providing support to families for up to 13 months after the patient’s death.
  • Hospice Aides (CNAs): Assist patients with personal care, activities of daily living, and provide companionship.

Wisconsin mandates specific training for all direct care staff. This includes 40 hours of initial orientation and training covering hospice philosophy, pain and symptom management, and emergency procedures, along with 12 hours of annual continuing education to ensure skills and knowledge remain current.

Section 7: Policies, Procedures, and Care Plans

Your operational rulebook is your set of policies and procedures. The DQA and CMS will scrutinize these documents during your initial survey to ensure they meet all regulatory standards. Wisconsin requires comprehensive written policies covering all aspects of your operation.

Key policy areas include:

  • Patient Rights and Grievance Procedures
  • Admission, Transfer, and Discharge Criteria
  • Interdisciplinary Group (IDG) Care Planning and Coordination
  • Pain and Symptom Management Protocols
  • Volunteer Program Management and Training
  • Bereavement Care Program Structure
  • Emergency Preparedness and Disaster Planning
  • Quality Assessment and Performance Improvement (QAPI) Program

Central to hospice care is the Individualized Plan of Care (POC). This document is created by the IDG in collaboration with the patient and family. Per state and federal rules, the POC must be reviewed and updated by the IDG at least every 15 days to reflect the patient’s changing needs and goals.

Section 8: Marketing and Referral Development

Hospice marketing is not about direct-to-consumer advertising. Instead, it is a professional, relationship-based effort focused on building trust with referral sources. Your success depends on your ability to become a reliable partner for healthcare professionals who identify and refer eligible patients.

Your primary referral sources in Wisconsin will include:

  • Hospital discharge planners and case managers
  • Oncologists, cardiologists, pulmonologists, and other specialist physicians
  • Primary care physicians and clinics
  • Skilled nursing facility administrators and directors of nursing
  • Assisted living community directors
  • Care managers at Managed Care Organizations (MCOs) like Inclusa and My Choice Wisconsin

Successful providers build their reputation on compliance, clinical excellence, responsiveness, and clear communication. Your ability to accept referrals quickly (within 24-48 hours), manage complex cases effectively, and provide excellent outcome documentation will be your most powerful marketing tools.

Section 9: Maintain Compliance and Prepare for Reviews

Achieving licensure is just the beginning. Ongoing compliance is essential for staying in business. Oversight in Wisconsin is conducted by multiple bodies. The Wisconsin DHS Division of Quality Assurance (DQA) will conduct unannounced surveys for state licensure compliance. For Medicare certification, surveys are performed by either state surveyors on behalf of CMS or by a national accrediting organization like the Community Health Accreditation Partner (CHAP) or The Joint Commission.

Inspections are rigorous and focus on ensuring patient safety and quality of care. Surveyors will review patient charts, interview staff and families, and observe care processes. Common deficiencies often relate to documentation, such as:

  • Incomplete or outdated patient care plans.
  • Errors in medication management documentation.
  • Insufficient documentation of staff training and competencies.
  • Lapses in documenting the required 15-day IDG meetings.

To stay prepared, implement a robust Continuous Quality Improvement (CQI) program. Regularly conduct self-audits of your charts and processes to identify and correct potential issues before a surveyor finds them. Maintaining audit-ready documentation at all times is the key to successful surveys and long-term operational health.

Section 10: Frequently Asked Questions

1. How long does it take to open a Hospice in Wisconsin?

Opening a hospice in Wisconsin, a process that includes state licensing from the DQA and the critical Medicare certification, typically takes 6 to 12 months. This timeline is highly dependent on the completeness of your application, your team’s readiness, and your ability to pass the initial surveys.

2. What licenses are required to operate a hospice in Wisconsin?

You must obtain a Hospice license from the Wisconsin DHS Division of Quality Assurance (DQA) by meeting the requirements in DHS 131. Critically, you must also achieve certification from the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) to be eligible for reimbursement from federal programs, which is the primary payer for hospice services.

3. What reimbursement is available for hospice services in Wisconsin?

Reimbursement primarily comes from Medicare and Wisconsin Medicaid, both of which pay on a per diem basis that varies by the level of care provided. Wisconsin Medicaid offers rates around $33-$35/day for routine home care. Medicare rates are generally higher, adjusted annually, and are the financial backbone of most agencies. You will also negotiate contracts and rates with Managed Care Organizations (MCOs) and other private insurers.

Conclusion

Starting a Hospice in Wisconsin is a challenging yet profoundly rewarding venture. It requires careful planning, a deep understanding of state and federal regulations, and unwavering operational discipline. The market presents a clear need, especially in rural communities and for specialized patient populations. Providers who invest in building a foundation of compliance, hiring and retaining excellent staff, and cultivating strong referral relationships are positioned for long-term success and the privilege of providing comfort and dignity to patients at the end of life.
